stories.metaTitle: Color Stories | EarthHue 色彩美学
stories.metaDescription: Where natural pigments come from — biology, history, the people behind them.
stories.title: Color Stories
stories.subtitle: Every pigment has a plant (or a microbe), a place, and a person behind it.

indigo.title: Indigo — Blue from a Leaf
indigo.lede: For three thousand years, blue came from one plant.
indigo.body: Indigofera leaves don't contain blue. They contain indican — a colourless precursor that oxidises into the deep indigo we recognise only after the leaf is crushed, fermented, and exposed to air.

saffron.title: Saffron — A Field of Red
saffron.lede: One hectare of saffron yields about ten kilograms of dried spice.
saffron.body: Each saffron crocus blooms for a single morning. The red threads are hand-picked from each flower — roughly 150 flowers per gram of dried saffron — which is why it's the most expensive spice on Earth.

beetroot.title: Beetroot — Pink That Won't Quit
beetroot.lede: Betanin is one of the rare natural pigments that survives heat.
beetroot.body: Most plant pigments break down when heated. Betanin — the pigment that makes beetroot red — actually becomes more vivid under heat, which is why it's the workhorse of pink and magenta in plant-based food.

spirulina.title: Spirulina — Blue from a Cyanobacterium
spirulina.lede: Phycocyanin gives spirulina its blue colour.
spirulina.body: Cyanobacteria were among the first oxygen-producing life forms on Earth. Phycocyanin, the blue pigment they share with spirulina, is one of the few natural blues that survives both heat and a neutral pH.

science.title: Science
science.subtitle: Short, sourced, jargon-free articles on the questions we get asked most.

natural-vs-synthetic.title: Natural vs synthetic dyes
natural-vs-synthetic.lede: They look the same on the page — but they aren't.
natural-vs-synthetic.body: Natural dyes come from plants, minerals, or microbes. Synthetic dyes are made from petrochemicals. The visible difference can be small, but the production footprint, regulatory framework, and skin-sensitisation profile often aren't.

sustainability.title: Are natural pigments sustainable?
sustainability.body: A crop grown for pigment can be a sink for regenerative agriculture, or a monoculture with high water use. Microbial (fermentation) pigments avoid most of the agricultural footprint, but they require energy for fermentation and downstream processing.

stability.title: Stability — why your dye faded
stability.lede: Light, pH, heat, oxygen, and metal ions.
stability.body: Most natural pigments are sensitive to one or more of these. A pigment that's stable in food (pH 4-6, opaque, no light) may fade in a clear cosmetic serum (pH 6-8, light-exposed). This is why formulation matters as much as pigment choice.

safety.title: Are natural pigments safer?
safety.lede: Generally, but "natural" isn't a regulatory category.
safety.body: Some natural pigments (e.g. lawone from henna) are potent skin sensitizers. Some synthetic pigments (e.g. iron oxides) are among the safest colorants we have. The label "natural" tells you origin, not safety.
